dct_description_sm:
Coastal island forest ecosystems in British Columbia face increasing
pressure from climate-driven stressors, yet the impact of residential
fragmentation on their functional resilience remains poorly understood.
This study compared land-use history and ecosystem health on Mudge
Island and Link Island in the Southern Gulf Islands of British Columbia
using a nine-year time series of Sentinel-2 multispectral satellite
imagery (2017–2025). A supervised Random Forest classification was
applied to quantify land cover composition and change, achieving an
overall accuracy of 77.7% (Kappa = 0.68). The Normalized Difference
Vegetation Index (NDVI) was calculated annually for both islands and
compared using a Welch's two-sample t-test. Results showed no
statistically significant difference in mean vegetation greenness
between the two islands (t(15.9) = −0.35, p = 0.733), with a mean
NDVI of 0.320 for Mudge Island and 0.303 for Link Island across the
study period. Forest cover on Mudge Island declined by 11.2 ha between
2018 and 2025, while Non-Forest Vegetation expanded by 25.7 ha. Link
Island remained stable across all land cover classes. Neither island
showed a measurable decline in vegetation productivity during the 2021
Pacific Northwest Heat Dome, indicating high ecological resistance to
short-term drought stress. These findings suggest that residential
fragmentation on Mudge Island has not yet reached a threshold that
compromises core ecosystem function. Multi-temporal satellite monitoring
provides a practical framework for tracking island forest stability
over time, with results offering baseline data for land managers working
to balance human land use with the preservation of resilient Coastal
Douglas-fir forests.
dct_title_s: Forest Resilience Under Residential Pressure: A Nine-Year Satellite Study of the Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia.
